title: What are Kearney, Roland Berger, L.E.K. and other strategy firms like to interview with?
description: A quick guide to interviewing at Kearney, Roland Berger, L.E.K., OC&C and Simon-Kucher: what makes each process distinctive.
hook: Kearney, Roland Berger, L.E.K., OC&C and Simon-Kucher all interview with live cases and fit questions much like MBB, but each has its own emphasis: operations at Kearney, private equity and life sciences at L.E.K., consumer and retail at OC&C, pricing at Simon-Kucher. Some add written or group cases. Prepare the core case skills once, then tailor your practice and your motivation to the firm's work.
body:
Why these firms are worth your attention

Beyond MBB and the Big Four sits a group of excellent strategy firms. They are often less crowded with applicants, they tend to have a clear specialism, and many people find the work or the culture a better fit. The interviews are no easier. The difference is that a generic answer to "why us?" fails faster, because each firm knows exactly what it is known for.

The firms at a glance

FirmKnown forWhat to expect
KearneyOperations and implementation alongside strategySeveral rounds of paired interviews, rising in seniority
Roland BergerStrategy work, with European roots and headquarters in MunichInterviews on motivation and numbers, plus case studies
L.E.K. ConsultingPrivate equity due diligence and life sciencesExperiential and case interviews; written cases in some offices
OC&CConsumer goods, retail, leisure and technologyCase interviews with a commercial, customer-focused flavour
Simon-KucherPricing and commercial growthCases where pricing and willingness to pay come up often

What each process looks like

Kearney

Processes vary by country, but Kearney's Belgian careers page, for example, describes three rounds of two interviews each: first with associates, then managers or principals, then partners. Expect operational cases (supply chains, procurement, cost) as often as classic growth questions, and stories that end in a measurable result.

Roland Berger

Roland Berger's selection process page for career starters lists an application with CV and cover letter, interviews about your motivation, numerical aptitude and how you handle criticism, and case studies. It stresses that there is no single correct way to solve a case, and suggests applying three to four months before your ideal start date.

L.E.K. Consulting

L.E.K. says its rounds mix experiential and case interviews, and that both quantitative and strategic cases are possible. You can apply to only one L.E.K. office per year, so choose carefully. Because so much of its work is commercial due diligence for investors, market sizing and "how fast will this market grow?" questions come up often. Candidate reports describe a written case in later rounds in some offices.

OC&C and Simon-Kucher

OC&C's sector list leads with consumer goods, retail, leisure and hospitality, and technology, media and telecoms, alongside private equity work. Simon-Kucher specialises in pricing, so expect pricing logic, customer segments and willingness to pay. For both, read some of the firm's published work before your interview.

A worked example: practise the firm's kind of case

Your structure should follow the client's decision, but the case you practise should match the firm's work. Here is an operations case of the sort a Kearney team might run.

Prompt: a parcel operator makes 2 million deliveries a year. 5% fail on the first attempt, and each repeat delivery costs $6. What is the problem worth?

  1. Failed first attempts: 2,000,000 × 5% = 100,000 a year.
  2. Cost: 100,000 × $6 = $600k a year.
  3. If a fix (delivery-time texts, safe-place options) cuts the failure rate to 3%: 60,000 × $6 = $360k, a saving of $240k a year before the cost of the fix.
  4. So-what: any fix costing well under $240k a year pays back. Next, split failures by cause (nobody home, wrong address, access problems) to see which fix to try first.
Weak: "They should improve their delivery process and communicate better with customers."
Strong: "Failures cost about $600k a year. Getting from 5% to 3% saves $240k, so I'd test delivery-time texts first, because 'nobody home' is likely the biggest cause, and check that with the data."

For an L.E.K.-style case, swap this for a market sizing and growth question; for Simon-Kucher, a price change. The complete guide to pricing cases and the market sizing guide cover both.

Common mistakes

  • Treating these firms as a back-up. Interviewers can tell. Give a reason tied to their specialism.
  • Ignoring the format. If an office uses written or group cases, practise them; our guide explains how.
  • Skipping the network. Smaller firms often weigh genuine contact heavily. A short conversation with someone in the practice gives you detail no website will.

Practise now

1. A Simon-Kucher-style question: a product sells 100 units at $100 with a variable cost of $60. The client raises the price 5% and loses 4% of volume. Does profit rise?

Show the answer

Before: 100 × ($100 − $60) = $4,000. After: 96 × ($105 − $60) = 96 × $45 = $4,320. Profit rises 8%. Volume could fall to $4,000 ÷ $45 ≈ 89 units, an 11% loss, before the increase stops paying.

2. Give a two-sentence answer to "Why L.E.K. rather than MBB?"

Show the answer

Something like: "I want to work on investment decisions, and due diligence puts the question 'is this market really growing?' at the centre of every project. When I spoke to a consultant in your London office about a recent diligence, the pace and the focus on one clear answer were exactly what I enjoyed in my valuation coursework." Then be ready to name the conversation honestly.

Where to practise next

See how these firms fit the wider market in our guide to the top consulting firms, and compare with the Oliver Wyman process. Details here were checked in November 2026; always confirm the format with the firm.
